label: History
value: Owen Ford is the son of Alice Selwyn.
unit: Owen Ford was born in Ontario, the son of Alice Selwyn and grandson of John Selwyn, the first schoolmaster of Glen St. Mary who built the little house of dreams. After working for years as a journalist and magazine writer, he suffered a severe bout of typhoid fever and was ordered to the seaside by his doctor to recuperate. In August, he went to Four Winds, boarders' accommodations having been arranged for him by Miss Cornelia Bryant at the home of Leslie Moore. Upon his arrival, Owen was struck by Leslie's extraordinary beauty, and soon fell deeply in love with her. Learning that her husband, Dick Moore, was hopelessly brain-damaged, Owen hid his feelings and poured his creative energies into writing a novel based on the 'life-book' of Captain Jim Boyd. After completing the manuscript in late summer, Owen confessed his agonizing, secret love for Leslie to Anne Blythe, before departing for Toronto without revealing his feelings to Leslie herself. Later, after Gilbert Blythe's medical intervention restored the memory of the man believed to be Dick Moore—revealing him to be his cousin, George Moore—Leslie became a free woman. Upon learning the news, Owen returned to Four Winds the following summer. He proposed to Leslie in Anne's garden, and they became engaged to be married in December. He also purchased the little house of dreams from the church trustees to serve as their summer home.

unit: Anthony Pye came to live in Avonlea after being taken in as an orphan nephew by Mr. and Mrs. George Pye. When Anne Shirley began her teaching career at the Avonlea school, Anthony was one of her new pupils and immediately displayed a sullen, defiant attitude toward her because she was a girl. He engaged in various pranks, including mocking Anne, making rude remarks about her hair, and dropping a mouse into her desk drawer. After the mouse incident, Anne lost her temper and gave him a whipping with her pointer. Contrary to her fears, the whipping earned Anthony's respect, and the next day he offered to carry her books and began behaving much better in school. When Anne resigned two years later to attend college, Anthony was so upset that he fought two pitched battles with other boys to vent his feelings, ultimately declaring that Anne was a good teacher after all.

Due to advancing age and heart trouble, the siblings decide to adopt an orphan boy to assist with farm work, but a misunderstanding results in the arrival of an eleven-year-old girl named Anne Shirley. Matthew is instantly won over by Anne's cheerful chatter on the drive from the station and quietly insists on keeping her. Over the next four years, he remains Anne's devoted confidant and champion, frequently spoiling her with treats and a fashionable dress with puffed sleeves for Christmas. When Anne passes her entrance examinations to Queen's Academy and subsequently wins the Avery Scholarship, Matthew takes immense pride in her achievements. Following her graduation, Matthew suffers a sudden, fatal heart attack upon reading news of the failure of the Abbey Bank, where his life savings were deposited, and he is buried in the Avonlea graveyard.

unit: Mrs. Rachel Lynde lived for over forty-five years in Lynde's Hollow, keeping a vigilant eye on all Avonlea happenings. When Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert decided to adopt a child, she initially strongly disapproved of bringing an orphan into Green Gables. Her first meeting with Anne Shirley resulted in a fierce explosion of temper when Rachel criticized the girl's looks, though she quickly accepted Anne's dramatic apology and grew quite fond of her over time. Following the death of her husband, Thomas Lynde, after a long illness, Rachel was forced to sell her mortgaged farm. Marilla Cuthbert invited her to move to Green Gables, where she set up her own quarters in the north gable. There, she assisted Marilla in managing the household and raising the young twins, Davy and Dora Keith, while Anne attended Redmond College. She continued her active involvement in the church Ladies' Aid Society and local affairs, remaining an indispensable pillar of the Avonlea community.

value: Miss Muriel Stacy forms an extra after-school class to prepare her pupils for the Queen's Academy Entrance examinations.
unit: Miss Muriel Stacy is hired as the first female schoolteacher in Avonlea, succeeding Mr. Phillips. She quickly wins the devotion of her pupils, including Anne Shirley, by introducing innovative educational methods such as nature field afternoons, physical culture exercises, and Friday recitation sessions. In November, she organizes a successful student concert to raise funds for a schoolhouse flag. Recognizing the potential of her advanced pupils, she forms an extra after-school class to prepare them for the Queen's Academy Entrance examinations. Although offered a teaching position in her home district, she declines it in order to remain in Avonlea and see her students through their final preparations. Under her guidance, her pupils make great progress, culminating in Anne Shirley and Gilbert Blythe tying for first place on the Island. After two years of teaching in Avonlea, Miss Stacy leaves for a new position and eventually marries in California.

To cope with her loneliness, she created a fantasy world of pretend tea parties, echoes, and an imaginary little dream-boy. She employed a series of young maidservants whom she collectively dubbed 'Charlotta.' When Anne Shirley and Diana Barry stumbled upon Echo Lodge, they quickly became close friends with Lavendar, drawn to her imaginative nature. Later, Anne brought Stephen's son, Paul Irving, to visit her, which deeply touched Lavendar. Through Anne's intervention, Stephen Irving returned to visit Lavendar after twenty-five years apart. The two reconciled, realizing their enduring love, and were married in the garden of Echo Lodge under the honeysuckle trellis. Following their wedding, they traveled to the Pacific coast before relocating to Boston, taking Paul and Charlotta the Fourth with them, while keeping Echo Lodge as a beloved summer home.

In his teens he ran away to sea, spending decades sailing the globe and experiencing shipwreck, mutiny, marooning, and battles. In his youth he loved a girl named Margaret, but she tragically drowned in a summer squall, an event that left an enduring mark on his life. Years later, while in Havana, he discovered an amnesiac sailor whom he believed to be Dick Moore, bringing him back to his wife Leslie. Retiring from the sea, Captain Jim became the keeper of the Four Winds Light, living a quiet life accompanied by his cat, the First Mate. When Anne Shirley and Gilbert Blythe moved into the old Selwyn house, he instantly recognized them as 'kindred spirits' belonging to 'the race that knows Joseph' and became a cherished friend. Later, when John Selwyn's grandson, Owen Ford, visited Four Winds, Captain Jim entrusted him with his manuscript 'life-book.' Owen adapted these real-life adventures into a highly successful novel. Shortly after receiving and reading the published book, Captain Jim passed away peacefully in his sleep at the lighthouse, his hands resting on his life-book.

passages.v01:c01:p0001: There are plenty of people, in Avonlea and out of it, who can attend closely to their neighbors’ business by dint of neglecting their own; but Mrs. Rachel Lynde was one of those capable creatures who can manage their own concerns and those of other folks into the bargain. She was a notable housewife; her work was always done and well done; she “ran” the Sewing Circle, helped run the Sunday-school, and was the strongest prop of the Church Aid Society and Foreign Missions Auxiliary. Yet with all this Mrs. Rachel found abundant time to sit for hours at her kitchen window, knitting “cotton warp” quilts—she had knitted sixteen of them, as Avonlea housekeepers were wont to tell in awed voices—and keeping a sharp eye on the main road that crossed the hollow and wound up the steep red hill beyond. Since Avonlea occupied a little triangular peninsula jutting out into the Gulf of St. Lawrence, with water on two sides of it, anybody who went out of it or into it had to pass over that hill road and so run the unseen gauntlet of Mrs. Rachel’s all-seeing eye.
passages.v01:c01:p0024: Mrs. Rachel prided herself on always speaking her mind; she proceeded to speak it now, having adjusted her mental attitude to this amazing piece of news.

Mrs. Rachel Lynde had gone too. Mrs. Rachel Lynde was a red-hot politician and couldn’t have believed that the political rally could be carried through without her, although she was on the opposite side of politics. So she went to town and took her husband—Thomas would be useful in looking after the horse—and Marilla Cuthbert with her. label: History
value: Aunt Jamesina brought the Sarah-cat.
unit: Aunt Jamesina lived alone in a large house after her only daughter, Elizabeth, married and left for a foreign mission field in India. Being lonely, she accepted an invitation to move to Kingsport and act as housekeeper and chaperone for her niece Stella Maynard and her friends Anne Shirley, Priscilla Grant, and Philippa Gordon at Patty's Place. She brought along her cats, the Sarah-cat and Joseph, and later adopted Rusty as well. Aunt Jamesina kept house for the girls during their remaining two years at Redmond College, offering them homely wisdom, cheerful company, and motherly care. When the girls graduated and Patty's Place was returned to its owners, Aunt Jamesina chose to remain in Kingsport or return home, taking all three cats with her to Green Gables before heading back.

She can’t help that! She was called Jamesina because her father, whose name was James, was drowned at sea a month before she was born. I always call her Aunt Jimsie. Well, her only daughter has recently married and gone to the foreign mission field. Aunt Jamesina is left alone in a great big house, and she is horribly lonesome. She will come to Kingsport and keep house for us if we want her, and I know you’ll both love her. The more I think of the plan the more I like it. We could have such good, independent times.
